title: What Size Is a Dryer Vent?
h1: What Size Is a Dryer Vent? Standard Dimensions Explained
description: Most residential dryer vents are 4 inches in diameter. Learn the right duct materials, transition hose rules and why the wrong size slows drying.
quick_answer: Standard residential dryer vents are 4 inches in diameter. That's the size most dryers are built for and the size the code is built around. The vent should be smooth metal duct, with a short metal transition hose behind the dryer. Don't reduce it to a smaller size, and don't assume a bigger duct will work better.
body:
Dryer vent size seems like a small detail, but getting it wrong causes a lot of problems. The 4-inch standard keeps air moving fast enough to carry lint all the way outside. Change the size or use the wrong material, and lint starts to settle inside the duct.

Why is 4 inches the standard?

Dryers are designed to push a certain volume of air at a certain speed. A 4-inch round duct matches that airflow. If the duct is smaller, the dryer can't push enough air through, so clothes take longer to dry and the dryer runs hotter. If the duct is larger, air slows down, and lint drops out and collects along the bottom.

Some compact, stacked or commercial dryers have different requirements, so always check the installation manual for your model.

What material should a dryer vent be?

  • Rigid metal duct. Smooth galvanized steel or aluminum is the best choice for the run inside walls, ceilings and attics. Smooth walls don't trap lint.
  • Semi-rigid aluminum. A good choice for the short connection between the dryer and the wall. It holds its shape better than foil.
  • Listed foil transition duct. Acceptable only for the short section behind the dryer, and only if it's listed for that use.
  • Plastic or vinyl hose. Never. It can melt, sag and burn, and it isn't allowed by code.

How long can the transition hose be?

The flexible connector behind the dryer should be no longer than 6 feet under California's mechanical code, and shorter is better. It shouldn't be concealed inside walls or ceilings. Keep it as straight as possible. Pushing the dryer tight against the wall can crush the hose and choke off airflow, which is one of the most common causes of slow drying we see.

What about the wall and roof caps?

The vent should end outside with a proper dryer vent hood. It needs a damper flap that opens when the dryer runs and closes to keep out pests and weather. Avoid hoods with screens, since screens catch lint and clog quickly. In many Southern California homes with interior laundry rooms, the vent exits through the roof, which needs a roof cap designed for dryer exhaust.

How should the vent be installed?

  1. Use 4-inch smooth metal duct for the full concealed run.
  2. Connect sections with the male end pointing in the direction of airflow, so joints don't catch lint.
  3. Seal joints with foil tape or clamps. Don't use screws that poke into the duct.
  4. Support the duct so it doesn't sag, especially in attics.
  5. Keep the total run within the code limit or the dryer manufacturer's venting chart, both of which account for elbows.
  6. End the vent outside, never in an attic, crawl space or garage.

How often should a dryer vent be cleaned?

Even a correctly sized vent collects lint over time. Once a year is a good rule for most households. Large families, homes that do laundry every day and vents with long runs or roof exits may need cleaning more often. Clean the lint screen after every load, and wash it with warm soapy water every few months, since dryer sheet residue can clog the mesh without you noticing.

What are the signs your dryer vent is the wrong size or setup?

  • Loads take longer than an hour or need a second cycle
  • The dryer or laundry room gets very hot
  • You smell something burning
  • Lint collects around the outside hood or behind the dryer
  • The outside flap barely opens when the dryer runs
  • The laundry room feels humid during drying

Any of these can point to a clogged, crushed or undersized vent. A blocked vent is a fire hazard, so it's worth looking into soon. If you have a gas dryer and ever smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside.

Our dryer vent team can clean the full run, replace a crushed or plastic hose with proper metal duct, and reroute vents that are too long or have too many turns.
faqs: Can I use a 3-inch dryer vent?

No. Reducing a residential dryer vent below 4 inches restricts airflow, makes the dryer work harder and raises the fire risk. Some compact dryers use a different connection, so check your manual, but standard dryers need 4-inch duct.
Not for a typical home dryer. A bigger duct slows the air down, which lets lint settle inside the vent. Stick with 4-inch duct unless the manufacturer says otherwise.
Is flexible foil dryer duct safe?

Only as a short, listed transition hose between the dryer and the wall. It should never be used for the concealed run inside walls, ceilings or attics. Smooth rigid metal is the safest choice for the main vent.
